lesson.title: Adding Voltages with Resistors: The Summing Amplifier
lesson.summary: The summing amplifier extends the inverting amplifier to multiple inputs, each through its own resistor into the same virtual ground node, producing an output equal to the weighted, inverted sum of the inputs, a direct application of the superposition principle.
lesson.body:
The summing amplifier takes the inverting amplifier from earlier in this unit and generalizes it to handle more than one input signal at once. Instead of a single input resistor, the circuit uses several, R1, R2, and so on, each carrying its own independent input voltage, V1, V2, and so on, all meeting at the same inverting input node. A single feedback resistor Rf connects the output back to that shared node, and the non-inverting input remains grounded, exactly as in the inverting amplifier.

Because V+ is still grounded and negative feedback is still present, the virtual ground condition still holds: V- sits at 0 volts. This is the key that makes multiple inputs tractable at all, since each input resistor now has a completely independent voltage across it, namely its own input voltage down to the shared 0 volt node, so each contributes its own current entirely independently of what the others are doing: I1 = V1 / R1, I2 = V2 / R2, and so on for however many inputs are present.

All of these currents merge at the summing node, and since the op-amp's infinite input impedance means none of it can escape into the amplifier itself, Kirchhoff's current law forces the entire sum to flow out through the single feedback resistor Rf: I_f = I1 + I2 + (any additional input currents). The output voltage follows the same reasoning used for the single-input inverting amplifier, Vout = negative I_f times Rf, giving Vout = negative (Rf/R1 times V1 + Rf/R2 times V2 + ...), a separate, independently scaled inverting-amplifier term for every input.

That structure, each input behaving exactly as if it were the only signal present, with the individual results simply added together, is the superposition principle at work, valid here because every part of the circuit, the op-amp under the ideal assumptions and the resistors, is linear. Formally, superposition would have you set every input but one to zero (replacing each inactive voltage source with a short to ground) and solve for the output contribution of the remaining source alone, then repeat for each input and add the results, and the result is identical to the direct current-summing argument above.

As a worked example, let Rf = 10 kilohms, with two inputs: R1 = 5 kilohms carrying V1 = 2 V, and R2 = 10 kilohms carrying V2 = 1 V. The output is Vout = negative (10 kilohms/5 kilohms times 2 V + 10 kilohms/10 kilohms times 1 V) = negative (2 times 2 + 1 times 1) = negative (4 + 1) = negative 5 V. Checking with the current-summing method: I1 = V1/R1 = 2 V / 5000 ohms = 0.0004 A (0.4 mA), and I2 = V2/R2 = 1 V / 10,000 ohms = 0.0001 A (0.1 mA). The total current through the feedback resistor is If = 0.4 mA + 0.1 mA = 0.5 mA, giving Vout = negative If times Rf = negative 0.0005 A times 10,000 ohms = negative 5 V, matching exactly.

Because each input channel can use a different resistor value, every input gets its own independent weight in the final sum, a feature exploited directly in audio mixing consoles, where each channel's resistor (or a variable version of one) sets that channel's contribution to the combined output, and in resistor-based digital-to-analog converters, where binary-weighted resistor values convert a set of digital bits into a single proportional analog voltage. With the summing amplifier, this unit's arc is complete: from the raw, unusable open-loop gain of a bare op-amp, through the feedback that tames it into a precise closed-loop gain, to the virtual short and virtual ground shortcuts that make hand analysis tractable, and finally to the three core building blocks, the inverting amplifier, the non-inverting amplifier and its voltage-follower limiting case, and now this multi-input extension of the inverting amplifier itself.
